arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE PAPER, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The corpus first prints this person at the American of 25 July 1835, column 3, so they are in the town's paper by 1834-12-17 and at no stated time before it; nothing reached says when they came. Last printed 1835-08-15.

persons.name: A. Garrett

occupation.note: THE TRADE IS THE PAPER'S. The corpus reads it as auction and commission merchant, auctioneer, at the American of 25 July 1835, column 3; the American of 15 August 1835, column 2; the Democrat of 17 December 1834, column 1; the Democrat of 24 December 1834, column 1. The residents vocabulary's nearest period-correct word for it is `auctioneer`, and where the corpus prints more than one trade they are all named here rather than reduced to the one the vocabulary could take.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'A. Gatren' and 'GARRETT,' and 'RRSTT' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the American of 25 July 1835, column 3; the American of 15 August 1835, column 2; the Democrat of 17 December 1834, column 1; the Democrat of 24 December 1834, column 1. The corpus associates the name with Dearborn Street, South Water Street; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `auctioneer` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 1 time, as “GARRETT A ET CO”, 1835-12-01: 1 federal land entry — W2SW sec 33 T38N R14E, 80.00 acres stated in all, for $100.00 (ls0693). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: GARRETT A ET CO matches A. Garrett: the residents layer holds exactly one person of the surname and the forename agrees as an initial only. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

resident_research.evidence_for: Independent of the post office in books, civic rolls, directories and more.
resident_research.evidence_against: The 1835 newspaper record gives only A. Garrett.
resident_research.notes: No candidate fact is asserted unless a source bridges the candidate to the 1835 Chicago record by more than name similarity.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name A. Garrett as a auctioneer at Chicago 4 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.
